passage: When a stretch of road was relit with white LED lamps in place of orange sodium ones, a volunteer survey counted bat passes along it for two summers. Passes by one common species rose sharply under the new lamps, which draw more insects than the old ones did. Passes by two slower-flying species, which hunt in shadow and are taken by owls in the open, fell to almost none and had not recovered by the end of the second summer.
prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The new lamps reduced the number of insects available to bats hunting along the relit road.
Bat activity along the relit road returned to its earlier level once the species had adjusted to the lamps.
The two slower-flying species left the relit road because the insects they hunt had been drawn elsewhere.
The change in lighting favored one bat species along the road while driving two others away from it.
correct_answer: The change in lighting favored one bat species along the road while driving two others away from it.
explanation: The survey reports two opposite outcomes under the same lamps: passes by the common species "rose sharply" while passes by the two slower-flying species "fell to almost none," which is what "favored one bat species along the road while driving two others away from it" states. "Reduced the number of insects available to bats hunting along the relit road" reverses the text, which says the new lamps draw more insects. "Returned to its earlier level once the species had adjusted to the lamps" is contradicted by the report that the two species had not recovered by the end of the second summer. And "because the insects they hunt had been drawn elsewhere" supplies a cause the text does not give; the reason offered for those species' absence is that they hunt in shadow and are taken by owls in the open.

passage: The flowers of a forest orchid smell faintly of rotting wood and are visited almost only by fungus gnats, which lay their eggs in decaying logs. A gnat that enters a flower leaves dusted with pollen, but the larvae that hatch from eggs laid inside it starve, since the orchid offers no tissue they can eat. A gnat that has once laid eggs in a flower goes on seeking out flowers of that same scent, so the orchid's deception is _____
prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: self-reinforcing, since the gnats it has already fooled are the ones most likely to visit it again.
self-limiting, since a gnat that has lost a brood in one flower will avoid others that smell of it.
incidental, since the gnats would visit the flowers whether or not they smelled of rotting wood.
costly, since the orchid must make more pollen than a flower that rewarded its visitors would.
correct_answer: self-reinforcing, since the gnats it has already fooled are the ones most likely to visit it again.
explanation: The text states that a gnat that has laid eggs in a flower goes on seeking flowers of that same scent, so being deceived once makes a gnat a better prospect for the next flower rather than a worse one, which is the reasoning behind "self-reinforcing, since the gnats it has already fooled are the ones most likely to visit it again." "Self-limiting, since a gnat that has lost a brood in one flower will avoid others that smell of it" asserts the opposite of the behavior the text reports. "Incidental, since the gnats would visit the flowers whether or not they smelled of rotting wood" is ruled out by the scent's role in drawing gnats that breed in decaying wood. And "costly, since the orchid must make more pollen" introduces a comparison of pollen output that the text never raises.

passage: Tin ingots recovered from a Bronze Age wreck carry isotope ratios that match no ore field in the eastern Mediterranean. One team proposes that the metal was mined far to the northwest and moved south along river corridors before it ever reached salt water, which would make the wreck the last leg of a much longer journey overland.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's proposal?
choices: Ingots recovered from a second wreck on the same stretch of coast were cast from ore with a wholly different isotopic signature.
Metalworkers along the eastern Mediterranean coast went on working their local tin deposits through the century of the wreck and for generations afterward.
The timber of the wreck's hull grew within a few days' sail of the stretch of coast where the ship went down.
Ingots matching the wreck's signature turn up at inland sites along a northwestern river corridor, in older layers the farther upriver they lie.
correct_answer: Ingots matching the wreck's signature turn up at inland sites along a northwestern river corridor, in older layers the farther upriver they lie.
explanation: The proposal has two parts, a northwestern source and a southward journey by river, and the finding that "ingots matching the wreck's signature turn up at inland sites along a northwestern river corridor, in older layers the farther upriver they lie" bears on both: it places the same metal on the route, and the age gradient gives the direction of travel. "A wholly different isotopic signature" at a second wreck says nothing about where the first wreck's metal came from. "Metalworkers along the eastern Mediterranean coast went on working their local tin deposits" concerns supply near the wreck and leaves the mismatch in ratios untouched. And where "the timber of the wreck's hull grew" dates the ship rather than the cargo, which is the thing whose origin is in dispute.

passage: A bird that swallows fruit whole disperses the seed when it later passes it, so how far the seed travels depends both on how long it is held in the gut and on how far the bird moves in that time. Researchers fed marked seeds from a single shrub to four bird species and then recorded, for each species, the median time a seed was retained and the median distance from the feeding station at which a marked seed was recovered. Dispersal distance did not rise in step with retention time; the hornbill, for instance, _____
prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

graphic.caption: Table 1. Median gut retention time and median dispersal distance for marked seeds fed to each of four bird species.

choices: retained seeds for the longest median time of the four species but carried them the shortest median distance.
carried seeds about as far as the barbet did, despite retaining them a median of 23 minutes longer.
retained seeds a median of 23 minutes longer than the barbet but carried them more than three times as far.
retained seeds more than twice as long as the bulbul but carried them a shorter median distance than the barbet.
correct_answer: retained seeds a median of 23 minutes longer than the barbet but carried them more than three times as far.
explanation: The table gives the hornbill 78 minutes against the barbet's 55, a difference of 23 minutes, and 410 meters against the barbet's 120, which is more than three times as far; that pairing of a modest gap in retention with a large gap in distance is what "retained seeds a median of 23 minutes longer than the barbet but carried them more than three times as far" reports, and it is the reason distance does not rise in step with retention. "Carried them the shortest median distance" is wrong on the second column, where the hornbill's 410 meters is the largest value in the table. "Carried seeds about as far as the barbet did" ignores the gap between 410 and 120 meters. And "a shorter median distance than the barbet" reverses that same comparison.

passage: Carved into the wall of a ninth-century temple are five ships, each with an outrigger and a tripod mast. The panels were long read as a record of the vessels that carried the island's rice trade. But the five hulls differ from one another in almost every particular except the mast, no two are shown in the same waters, and one sails past a fish larger than itself. The panels may say less about what sailed the strait than about what the carvers took a ship to be.
prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The temple's ship panels may be better evidence of a convention for depicting ships than of the vessels then in use.
The temple's ship panels record the range of vessels that carried the island's rice trade more fully than was once recognized.
The temple's ship panels were cut by carvers who had little chance to observe seagoing vessels at first hand.
The temple's ship panels show waters that the island's traders were unlikely to have sailed in the ninth century.
correct_answer: The temple's ship panels may be better evidence of a convention for depicting ships than of the vessels then in use.
explanation: The text sets a documentary reading of the panels against a second one and closes by preferring the second: the panels tell us "what the carvers took a ship to be," which is what "may be better evidence of a convention for depicting ships than of the vessels then in use" states, and the shared tripod mast amid otherwise unlike hulls is the detail that supports it. "Record the range of vessels ... more fully than was once recognized" restates the documentary reading the text is arguing against. "Carvers who had little chance to observe seagoing vessels at first hand" is a claim about the carvers' access that the text never makes. And "waters that the island's traders were unlikely to have sailed" fastens on the settings rather than the ships, and the oversized fish is offered as a sign of convention, not as a claim about which straits were sailed.

passage: On a rocky shore a periwinkle grazes across bare rock at high tide and is back in the same crevice before the water drops. The snail travels in darkness, and the crevice has no distinguishing shape or smell of its own. One researcher proposes that the snail finds its way home by retracing the mucus trail it laid down on the way out.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the researcher's proposal?
choices: Snails whose crevice is filled in while they graze return to the spot where it stood and settle there.
Snails that graze farther from their crevice take correspondingly longer to get back to it before the tide drops.
Snails whose outward trail is wiped from the rock behind them fail to find the crevice they set out from.
Snails that cross rock recently traveled by another snail follow that snail's trail rather than their own.
correct_answer: Snails whose outward trail is wiped from the rock behind them fail to find the crevice they set out from.
explanation: If the trail is what the snail follows, then removing the trail should remove the ability, and that is exactly the result in "snails whose outward trail is wiped from the rock behind them fail to find the crevice they set out from." "Snails whose crevice is filled in while they graze return to the spot where it stood" shows only that the snail can locate a position, leaving open every means by which it might do so. "Take correspondingly longer to get back" follows from distance alone and would hold under any method of navigation. And snails that "follow that snail's trail rather than their own" would show that mucus is followed but not that it is how a snail gets home, since a foreign trail leads somewhere else.

passage: A thicket of sea buckthorn on a coastal dune has produced no seedlings in forty years, yet it has not shrunk: new stems rise each spring from the roots of older ones. Rabbits graze the dune heavily, and a seedling bitten off at the sand cannot recover, while a root sprout that is bitten can. A census found stems of many ages but no more genetic variation across the whole thicket than within a single shrub.
prompt: Based on the text, what is most likely true of the new stems that rise in the thicket each spring?
choices: They are seedlings that escape the rabbits by coming up among the older stems.
They are shoots of the same individuals as the older stems rather than new plants.
They survive the rabbits better than the older stems do because they are bitten less often.
They establish themselves from seed in the years when the rabbits graze the dune lightly.
correct_answer: They are shoots of the same individuals as the older stems rather than new plants.
explanation: The census found stems of many ages carrying no more genetic variation than a single shrub, which means the new stems are not new individuals, and the text supplies the mechanism in the root sprouts that come up where seedlings cannot survive; that is the reading in "they are shoots of the same individuals as the older stems rather than new plants." "Seedlings that escape the rabbits by coming up among the older stems" is ruled out twice over, by the forty years without seedlings and by the uniform genetics. "They survive the rabbits better than the older stems do because they are bitten less often" mistakes what the text says about sprouts, which is that a bitten sprout recovers, not that it is bitten less. And "establish themselves from seed in the years when the rabbits graze the dune lightly" would produce stems that differ genetically from one another, which the census did not find.

passage: A frog calling from the forest floor must be heard through litter that absorbs much of the call. Researchers played a recorded call from four heights above the litter and measured, at two distances, how much of the energy put into it survived. The results indicate that the height from which males of this species actually call is not the height from which a call carries best: _____
prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

graphic.caption: Table 1. Percent of the emitted energy remaining at two distances from the speaker, by the height above the litter from which the call was played. Males of this species call from 0.1 m.

choices: at 20 m, 28 percent of the energy played from 0.1 m remained, against 74 percent of that played from 1.0 m.
at 20 m, 28 percent of the energy played from 0.1 m remained, against 82 percent of that played from 2.0 m.
at 5 m, 71 percent of the energy played from 0.1 m remained, against 96 percent of that played from 0.4 m.
at 5 m, 64 percent of the energy played from 0.1 m remained, against 88 percent of that played from 0.4 m.
correct_answer: at 20 m, 28 percent of the energy played from 0.1 m remained, against 74 percent of that played from 1.0 m.
explanation: The table gives 28 percent remaining at 20 m for a call played from the height males use and 74 percent for one played from 1.0 m, so "at 20 m, 28 percent of the energy played from 0.1 m remained, against 74 percent of that played from 1.0 m" is the reading that shows the species' own height is not the best one. "Against 82 percent of that played from 2.0 m" inflates a figure the table gives as 55. "At 5 m, 71 percent of the energy played from 0.1 m remained, against 96 percent of that played from 0.4 m" starts from the right value for 0.1 m and then reports 96 where the table gives 88. And "at 5 m, 64 percent of the energy played from 0.1 m remained, against 88 percent of that played from 0.4 m" has the 0.4 m figure right and the 0.1 m figure wrong, since 71 percent remained at that distance.

passage: A core drawn from a mountain lake holds pollen from the surrounding slopes in yearly layers. Through one stretch of the core, pine pollen falls sharply while charcoal rises; through the stretch above it, charcoal disappears and oak pollen rises. Pine sheds far more pollen per tree than oak does, and pollen that lands on the lake sinks within the season it falls. A modest loss of pines from the slopes could therefore appear in the core as _____
prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: a rise in charcoal out of proportion to the number of trees that actually burned.
a fall in pine grains out of proportion to the loss of trees on the slopes.
a fall in oak grains matching the fall in pine grains layer for layer.
a rise in the total number of grains that the affected layers contain.
correct_answer: a fall in pine grains out of proportion to the loss of trees on the slopes.
explanation: Because each pine contributes far more grains to a layer than each oak does, the count is weighted toward pines, so losing a few of them removes a disproportionate share of the grains; that is the reasoning behind "a fall in pine grains out of proportion to the loss of trees on the slopes." "A rise in charcoal out of proportion to the number of trees that actually burned" transfers the argument to charcoal, for which the text gives no differential production rate. "A fall in oak grains matching the fall in pine grains layer for layer" contradicts the core, where oak holds steady and then rises. And "a rise in the total number of grains that the affected layers contain" runs the wrong way, since removing the heaviest pollen producer lowers the total rather than raising it.

passage: The surviving typescripts of a mid-century novel show its author cutting almost nothing. Scenes that the published book gives in two pages run to two pages in the earliest draft, with the same clauses in the same order. What the typescripts do show is insertion. Between the first draft and the second, the narrator acquires a habit of correcting herself, and sixty of these corrections are added in the margins of pages otherwise untouched.
prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The published novel differs from its earliest draft chiefly in the order in which its scenes are set out.
The novel's author drafted her scenes at close to their final length and then revised by paring away detail.
The novel's narrator was given her self-correcting manner only after the author had settled on an ending.
The novel's revision consisted less of cutting than of adding one new habit to the narrator's voice.
correct_answer: The novel's revision consisted less of cutting than of adding one new habit to the narrator's voice.
explanation: The typescripts are described as showing almost no cutting and a great deal of one particular insertion, the narrator's self-correction, which is what "consisted less of cutting than of adding one new habit to the narrator's voice" states. "Chiefly in the order in which its scenes are set out" is contradicted by the report that the same clauses appear in the same order. "Revised by paring away detail" names the very activity the typescripts show the author not doing. And "only after the author had settled on an ending" brings in the ending, which the text never mentions; the sequence it gives runs between the first draft and the second.

passage: Potters in two villages on the same river finish their storage jars with a rim that is rolled in the upstream village and folded in the downstream one. Sherds from the downstream village show the rolled rim appearing gradually over four decades and the folded rim fading out. One team argues that the change came not from potters admiring and copying an upstream style but from women marrying downstream, each bringing with her the technique she had learned as a girl.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the team's argument?
choices: Jars with rolled rims from the downstream village are finished more finely than the jars with folded rims are.
In the downstream village the rolled rim appears first in the households whose burials hold ornaments of upstream make.
Potters in the upstream village had been rolling their rims for some decades before the downstream change began.
Jars with rolled rims are found throughout the downstream village's rubbish deposits from the first decade of the change.
correct_answer: In the downstream village the rolled rim appears first in the households whose burials hold ornaments of upstream make.
explanation: The team's argument turns on people moving rather than a style spreading, so the useful evidence ties the new rim to particular incomers, and "the rolled rim appears first in the households whose burials hold ornaments of upstream make" does that by putting the technique and a person of upstream origin in the same house. "Finished more finely than the jars with folded rims are" speaks to the rim's appeal, which is the copying explanation the team rejects. "Had been rolling their rims for some decades before the downstream change began" establishes only that the technique existed upstream first, which both explanations require. And rolled rims "found throughout the downstream village's rubbish deposits from the first decade" points away from the argument, since arrival by marriage predicts the rim showing up in some households before others.

passage: A cut mark left by a stone tool and a tooth mark left by a carnivore can sit on the same bone, and whichever lies on top was made second. Where people took carcasses that carnivores had already opened, cut marks should overlie tooth marks; where people had first access, the reverse should hold. Every long-bone fragment from four successive layers of one rock shelter was scored for the two relations. The marks are consistent with scavenging in the shelter's later layers but not in its earlier ones: _____
prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

graphic.caption: Table 1. Long-bone fragments scored in each layer and the number carrying each overlap relation. Fragments carrying neither relation are counted in the first column only.

choices: 47 of the 240 fragments scored in Layer 2 carry a cut mark over a tooth mark, against 24 of the 212 in Layer 3.
58 of the 86 fragments scored in Layer 1 carry a cut mark over a tooth mark, against 24 of the 212 in Layer 3.
150 of the 240 fragments scored in Layer 2 carry a cut mark over a tooth mark, against 24 of the 212 in Layer 3.
20 of the 96 fragments scored in Layer 1 carry a cut mark over a tooth mark, against 12 of the 86 in Layer 4.
correct_answer: 150 of the 240 fragments scored in Layer 2 carry a cut mark over a tooth mark, against 24 of the 212 in Layer 3.
explanation: The scavenging signature is the cut mark lying on top, and the table puts that relation on 150 of the 240 fragments in Layer 2 against only 24 of the 212 in Layer 3, which is the contrast between a later layer and an earlier one that the statement needs; "150 of the 240 fragments scored in Layer 2 carry a cut mark over a tooth mark, against 24 of the 212 in Layer 3" reports it. "47 of the 240 fragments scored in Layer 2" takes Layer 2's figure from the tooth-over-cut column, which leaves the later layer looking barely different from the earlier one. "58 of the 86 fragments scored in Layer 1" borrows both of Layer 4's numbers and attaches them to Layer 1, a layer the table gives 61 of 96. And "20 of the 96 fragments scored in Layer 1 carry a cut mark over a tooth mark, against 12 of the 86 in Layer 4" has Layer 1's total right but its count from the wrong column, so it reports the shallowest layer as barely scavenged at all.

passage: In 1847 a naturalist surveying a chain of salt lakes kept a daily journal that his editors later mined for its descriptions of birds. A recent study argues that the journal's real subject is elsewhere: what it records most consistently is how little the writer could trust the people on whom he depended for everything he was not able to see for himself.
prompt: Which quotation from the journal most effectively illustrates the study's claim?
choices: "The crust at the lake's rim glittered until noon and then went dull."
"My guide says the water rises every seventh year; he was not here seven years ago."
"Flamingos stood in the shallows all morning, and I counted what I could count."
"I set down in the evening what the day has left me, which is never the whole of it."
correct_answer: "My guide says the water rises every seventh year; he was not here seven years ago."
explanation: The claim is specifically about the writer's informants, and "My guide says the water rises every seventh year; he was not here seven years ago" both reports what an informant told him and, in the same breath, gives the reason the guide was in no position to know it. "The crust at the lake's rim glittered until noon" is description the writer made himself and involves no informant at all. "I counted what I could count" and "which is never the whole of it" do concern the limits of the record, but the limits they name are the writer's own reach and memory, not the reliability of anyone he was relying on.

passage: A sourdough starter kept at room temperature is dominated by one yeast and two lactic acid bacteria; moved to a cooler shelf, the same starter shifts within a week to a community in which one of the bacteria nearly vanishes. Cultured on their own, both bacteria grow at both temperatures, and the yeast grows faster in the cold than either. The bacterium that vanishes lives on a sugar the yeast releases, and the bacterium that persists takes the same sugar and grows faster in the cold, so _____
prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the cold must act on the vanishing bacterium directly rather than through anything the yeast does.
the yeast must release less of that sugar in the cold than the two bacteria together take up.
its disappearance is more likely a matter of competition for that sugar than of the cold itself.
the surviving bacterium must supply the yeast with something the vanished one could not.
correct_answer: its disappearance is more likely a matter of competition for that sugar than of the cold itself.
explanation: Cultured alone the vanishing bacterium grows perfectly well in the cold, so the cold by itself does not account for its loss; what changes on the cool shelf is that a rival for the one sugar it depends on grows faster, which is the reading in "more likely a matter of competition for that sugar than of the cold itself." "The cold must act on the vanishing bacterium directly" is refused by the solo cultures. "The yeast must release less of that sugar in the cold" runs against the report that the yeast grows faster there, and nothing in the text measures uptake against release. And "must supply the yeast with something the vanished one could not" invents an exchange running back toward the yeast that the text does not describe.

passage: Histories of the style place its beginning in the recordings of 1926, where a two-beat accompaniment gives way to four. A second account observes that the shift is audible three years earlier in the playing of pianists working outside the recording studios, where the instrument's bass register had made the older accompaniment awkward to sustain. What 1926 supplies, on this reading, is not the innovation but the date at which the bands around those pianists stopped lagging behind them.
prompt: According to the text, what does the second of the two accounts take the 1926 recordings to show?
choices: They register in ensemble playing a change that pianists had made already.
They preserve the last recorded examples of the two-beat accompaniment.
They mark the point at which pianists gave up the two-beat accompaniment.
They catch ensembles resisting a change that pianists had begun three years before.
correct_answer: They register in ensemble playing a change that pianists had made already.
explanation: The second account keeps 1926 as a real date but reassigns what it dates, calling those sides the moment the ensembles caught up with their pianists, which is what "they register in ensemble playing a change that pianists had made already" says. "They preserve the last recorded examples of the two-beat accompaniment" turns the recordings into an endpoint for the older style, where the text has them introducing the newer one to ensemble playing. "They mark the point at which pianists gave up the two-beat accompaniment" puts the pianists' change in 1926, three years later than the account places it. And "they catch ensembles resisting a change that pianists had begun three years before" makes the ensembles holdouts in that year, where the account has them adopting the change rather than refusing it.

passage: A transect run up a forested ridge recorded the number of resident bird species found in bands at four elevations. The researchers had expected the count to fall steadily with height as the forest thinned and the growing season shortened. The transect instead found that _____
prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the figure to complete the statement?

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Number of resident bird species recorded in each elevation band along the transect.

choices: the count fell from 44 species at 400 m to 22 at 800 m before rising again.
the count was 39 species at 1,200 m and 44 species at 1,600 m.
the count rose from 31 species at 400 m to 44 at 800 m before falling.
the count at 800 m, 31 species, was the same as the count at 400 m.
correct_answer: the count rose from 31 species at 400 m to 44 at 800 m before falling.
explanation: A steady fall with height is what the figure refuses: the count goes up from the lowest band to the second before it turns down, which is what "the count rose from 31 species at 400 m to 44 at 800 m before falling" reports. "The count fell from 44 species at 400 m to 22 at 800 m before rising again" turns the transect upside down, giving the 400 m band the 800 m figure and the 800 m band the figure for the highest band. "The count was 39 species at 1,200 m and 44 species at 1,600 m" reads the 1,200 m band correctly and then gives the highest band 44 species, where the figure gives it 22. And "the count at 800 m, 31 species, was the same as the count at 400 m" moves the 400 m value up one band and flattens the rise that the figure shows.

passage: Twelve carved gaming pieces recovered from a coastal settlement were long assumed to have been made where they were found. Isotope ratios in the ivory, however, match walrus hunted in waters a thousand miles to the west, and the tool marks on all twelve resemble one another more closely than any of them resembles the marks on bone carved locally in the same period.
prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The gaming pieces were cut from local ivory but worked by a craftsman who had trained far away.
The gaming pieces were carved at the coastal settlement from ivory that had been traded a long way.
The gaming pieces were made from a material that the settlement's own carvers could not work well.
The gaming pieces were both sourced and carved far from the settlement where they were recovered.
correct_answer: The gaming pieces were both sourced and carved far from the settlement where they were recovered.
explanation: Two lines of evidence point the same way: the isotopes put the ivory a thousand miles off, and the tool marks group the twelve with one another rather than with local carving, so the material and the workmanship are both foreign, which is what "both sourced and carved far from the settlement where they were recovered" states. "Cut from local ivory" contradicts the isotope result. "Carved at the coastal settlement from ivory that had been traded a long way" accepts the isotopes but ignores the tool marks, which is the assumption the text is overturning. And "a material that the settlement's own carvers could not work well" makes a claim about local skill that the comparison of tool marks does not support.

passage: Nails drawn from a single eighteenth-century forge run from brittle to tough, and the brittle ones come from the bottom of the scrap heap. The iron's carbon content is the same throughout the heap. One metallurgist proposes that the difference lies not in the metal but in how long each nail was held at heat before being hammered, the bottom of the heap having been made at the end of the day, when the fire was banked.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the metallurgist's proposal?
choices: Tough nails reheated and held at a low heat before hammering come out as brittle as those from the bottom of the heap.
Brittle nails from the heap carry traces of phosphorus that the tough nails from the same heap do not.
The forge's fire was banked each evening to a temperature some two hundred degrees below its working heat, on every day of the year.
Nails from a second forge of similar design show the same range of brittleness in much the same proportion.
correct_answer: Tough nails reheated and held at a low heat before hammering come out as brittle as those from the bottom of the heap.
explanation: The proposal is that heat treatment rather than composition decides brittleness, and "tough nails reheated and held at a low heat before hammering come out as brittle as those from the bottom of the heap" tests it directly by changing the treatment while holding the metal fixed. "Traces of phosphorus that the tough nails from the same heap do not" carry works against the proposal, since it locates the difference in the metal after all. "Banked each evening to a temperature some two hundred degrees below its working heat" establishes only that the fire cooled, which is the premise of the proposal rather than evidence for its effect on the iron. And the same range of brittleness at "a second forge of similar design" shows the pattern is not peculiar to one shop without saying what produces it.

passage: Fiddler crabs riddle a salt marsh with burrows, and the cordgrass standing within a few centimeters of a burrow mouth grows taller than the grass farther off. Marsh soils are waterlogged, and cordgrass roots do poorly where oxygen is scarce. A burrow open to the air carries oxygen down into the soil around it, so the taller grass beside the burrows is best explained by _____
prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the crabs' habit of grazing on the shorter grass that grows between the burrows.
the extra light that reaches a plant standing at the edge of an opening in the soil.
the salt the crabs carry up out of the burrow and deposit around its mouth.
the oxygen a burrow admits to soil in which the roots would otherwise struggle.
correct_answer: the oxygen a burrow admits to soil in which the roots would otherwise struggle.
explanation: The text supplies a limit on growth, scarce oxygen at the roots, and a means of relieving it, a burrow open to the air, and the taller grass sits exactly where that relief reaches, which is the explanation in "the oxygen a burrow admits to soil in which the roots would otherwise struggle." "The crabs' habit of grazing on the shorter grass" invents a feeding behavior the text does not report and would in any case explain short grass rather than tall. "The extra light that reaches a plant standing at the edge of an opening" appeals to a factor the text never names as limiting. And "the salt the crabs carry up out of the burrow" would make conditions beside a burrow worse rather than better for the grass.

passage: The widths of annual rings in pines growing on a dry terrace above a river track the river's flow closely enough that the rings have been used to reconstruct flows for centuries before any gauge was installed. The pines draw on groundwater fed by the same snowpack that feeds the river. Since an upstream dam began holding back the spring melt, however, the correspondence between ring width and gauged flow has weakened, which suggests that _____
prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the rings have been recording the snowpack rather than the flow a gauge measures.
the pines have begun drawing on water from some source other than the snowpack.
the reconstruction is unreliable for the centuries before the gauges were installed.
the dam has cut the total amount of water reaching the terrace's groundwater.
correct_answer: the rings have been recording the snowpack rather than the flow a gauge measures.
explanation: Ring width and gauged flow agreed while both followed the snowpack, and they parted when the dam broke the link between snowpack and gauged flow, which points to the snowpack as what the rings were tracking all along: "the rings have been recording the snowpack rather than the flow a gauge measures." "Drawing on water from some source other than the snowpack" would explain a breakdown too, but the dam holds back the melt rather than the groundwater, and the text gives the pines no second source. "Unreliable for the centuries before the gauges were installed" gets the consequence backward, since in undammed centuries snowpack and flow moved together. And "cut the total amount of water reaching the terrace's groundwater" describes a dam that diverts water away, where this one delays the melt.

passage: Participants studied a list of word pairs and were tested after one of four delays. Half studied the list once; half studied it twice, with an hour between sessions. One account holds that the second session simply lifts recall by a fixed amount whenever the test comes; another holds that it slows the rate at which the pairs are lost. The results favor the second account: _____
prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

graphic.caption: Table 1. Percent of word pairs recalled at each delay by the group that studied the list once and the group that studied it twice.

choices: the twice-studied group's advantage grew from 6 percentage points at 10 minutes to 18 points at 1 week.
the twice-studied group's advantage grew from 6 percentage points at 10 minutes to 30 points at 1 month.
the twice-studied group's advantage grew from 14 percentage points at 1 day to 44 points at 1 month.
the twice-studied group's advantage grew from 6 percentage points at 10 minutes to 34 points at 1 month.
correct_answer: the twice-studied group's advantage grew from 6 percentage points at 10 minutes to 30 points at 1 month.
explanation: A fixed lift and a slower rate of loss are told apart by what happens to the gap between the groups as the delay grows, and the table gives that gap as 78 against 72 at 10 minutes and 44 against 14 at 1 month, which is what "the twice-studied group's advantage grew from 6 percentage points at 10 minutes to 30 points at 1 month" reports. "To 18 points at 1 week" takes the gap at 1 day and puts it at 1 week, where the table makes it 28. "From 14 percentage points at 1 day to 44 points at 1 month" is built from two recall figures rather than two gaps: 14 and 44 are what the once-studied and twice-studied groups recalled at 1 month. And "to 34 points at 1 month" reports the twice-studied group's own fall across the four delays, from 78 percent to 44, rather than its advantage over the other group.

passage: The two texts of an 1857 agreement were signed on the same day, and neither was labeled a translation of the other. Where one grants the right to "pass over" a tract, the other uses a verb that in ordinary usage covers both passing over and settling on. Later disputes turned on which text governed. The negotiators' own notes show that the question was raised during the talks and left where it stood, each side recording that its text said what it meant.
prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The agreement's two texts diverge because one was translated in haste from the other on the day of signing.
The agreement's negotiators argued over a verb whose sense neither side's language was able to render exactly.
The agreement's later disputes grew out of a passage the negotiators had overlooked while drafting it.
The agreement's two texts differ in a way the negotiators noticed and declined to settle before signing.
correct_answer: The agreement's two texts differ in a way the negotiators noticed and declined to settle before signing.
explanation: The text establishes both that the two versions say different things about the same right and that the notes record the discrepancy being raised and then left as it was, which together give "differ in a way the negotiators noticed and declined to settle before signing." "Translated in haste from the other on the day of signing" is ruled out at the start, where neither text is a translation of the other. "A verb whose sense neither side's language was able to render exactly" makes the problem a limit of the languages, while the notes make it a choice not to resolve. And "a passage the negotiators had overlooked" is contradicted by the same notes, which show the passage was raised in the talks.

passage: A night-flying moth pollinates one orchid on a mountainside, and that orchid's scent carries a compound found in no other flower there. Females of the moth lay their eggs only on a shrub that grows nowhere near the orchid. One team proposes that the moth's attraction to the compound arose first as a response to a chemical the shrub gives off, and that the orchid is exploiting a preference that was already in place.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the team's proposal?
choices: The orchid's scent carries the compound at far higher concentrations than the shrub's leaves release it.
Moths from a valley where the orchid does not grow are drawn to the compound as strongly as moths from the mountain.
Moths reared on the shrub visit the orchid more readily than moths reared on an unrelated plant do.
The shrub and the orchid are the only plants on the mountain known to give off the compound, and both do so after dark.
correct_answer: Moths from a valley where the orchid does not grow are drawn to the compound as strongly as moths from the mountain.
explanation: If the preference came first and the orchid is exploiting it, the preference should be present in moths that have never encountered the orchid, which is what "moths from a valley where the orchid does not grow are drawn to the compound as strongly as moths from the mountain" shows. "At far higher concentrations than the shrub's leaves release it" compares the two sources' output and is consistent with the attraction having arisen either way. "Moths reared on the shrub visit the orchid more readily" points to experience during rearing rather than to a preference that predates the orchid. And that both plants "give off the compound, and both do so after dark" establishes the overlap the proposal starts from without saying which came first.

passage: Sawfly larvae develop inside galls on willow leaves, and a willow's resistance to them is usually reported as galls per hundred leaves. A nursery grows two varieties beside each other at three sites. If one variety were resistant and the other susceptible, the difference between them ought to hold in the same direction from site to site. The counts instead show that _____
prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the figure to complete the statement?

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Galls per hundred leaves. The bar labeled A-1 is variety 1 at Site A, A-2 is variety 2 at Site A, and so on for Sites B and C.

choices: variety 1 carried 40 galls per hundred leaves at Site A but 15 at Site B, where variety 2 carried 38.
variety 1 carried 12 galls per hundred leaves at Site A but 26 at Site C, where variety 2 carried 24.
variety 1 carried 12 galls per hundred leaves at Site A but 38 at Site B, where variety 2 carried 15.
variety 2 carried 24 galls per hundred leaves at Site A but 40 at Site C, where variety 1 carried 26.
correct_answer: variety 1 carried 12 galls per hundred leaves at Site A but 38 at Site B, where variety 2 carried 15.
explanation: A variety that is resistant everywhere cannot be the lighter-infested of the pair at one site and the heavier at another, and the figure shows variety 1 carrying 12 galls per hundred leaves at Site A, where variety 2 carries 40, and 38 at Site B, where variety 2 carries 15; "variety 1 carried 12 galls per hundred leaves at Site A but 38 at Site B, where variety 2 carried 15" reports that reversal. "Variety 1 carried 40 galls per hundred leaves at Site A but 15 at Site B, where variety 2 carried 38" swaps the two varieties at both sites. "Variety 1 carried 12 ... but 26 at Site C, where variety 2 carried 24" has Site A right and then swaps the pair at Site C, where the figure gives variety 1 twenty-four and variety 2 twenty-six. And "variety 2 carried 24 galls per hundred leaves at Site A but 40 at Site C" moves variety 2's Site A figure of 40 to Site C and puts Site C's variety 1 figure in its place.
